Effect of protection zone on the dynamics of a diffusion-advection population-toxicant model

This work was partially supported by grants from National Science Foundation of China (12371503, 12071382), Natural Science Foundation of Chongqing (CSTB2022NSCQ-MSX0284, CSTB2024NSCQ-MSX0992).
Jing Gao    Xiaoli Wang    Guohong Zhang Note: Corresponding Author. Email: wxl711@swu.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Southwest University,
Abstract

This paper develops and analyzes a diffusion-advection model coupling population dynamics with toxicant transport, incorporating a boundary protection zone. For both upstream and downstream protection zone configurations, we investigate the combined influence of protected zones and key ecological factors on population persistence or extinction. Employing monotone dynamical system theory and eigenvalue analysis, we establish the global dynamics of the population-toxicant coexistence equilibrium. Furthermore, we characterize the parameter dependence governing the stability of the toxicant-only steady state, specifically examining the protected zone length, toxicant effect coefficient on population growth, per-unit contaminant discharge rate, toxicant input rate, diffusion/advection rates, and population natural growth rate. Finally, numerical simulations reveal the complex interplay between the protection zone and toxicant advection rate in significantly shaping population persistence domains.

Keywords: Reaction-diffusion-advection; Protection zone; Population persistence; Monotone dynamical system; Toxicant

1 Introduction

Aquatic ecosystems constitute vital natural environments essential for human survival. However, rapid industrialization and economic growth have continuously intensified environmental pressures. Large quantities of toxic substances, including untreated industrial wastewater, chemical detergents, and plastic fragments, are discharged directly into rivers and lakes, posing significant threats to aquatic organisms and severely disrupting ecosystem balance. As water pollution worsens globally, its remediation has become a critical issue of widespread concern.

Ecologists and mathematicians have employed mathematical modeling to investigate the long-term sustainability of aquatic communities and ecosystems [8, 11, 23]. Various models, including ordinary differential equation models [6, 7, 10] and matrix population models [4, 8, 22], have been developed. However, these models often inadequately account for the significant influence of hydrological and physical properties of water bodies on population dynamics and toxicant behavior. In river ecosystems, once introduced, toxicants disperse via both diffusion and advective transport. Furthermore, given that the longitudinal scale of rivers typically far exceeds their cross-sectional dimensions, toxicants rapidly achieve cross-sectional homogeneity upon entering the flow. Reflecting this characteristic, advection-diffusion-reaction models in the horizontal dimension are commonly adopted for theoretical studies [20, 26, 31]. While such models for contaminated rivers effectively predict the spatiotemporal evolution of pollutants and their environmental impacts, they have paid less attention to the potential role of toxicants in actively shaping population dynamics.

To specifically study the effects of environmental toxicants on populations in polluted rivers, Zhou and Huang [32] develop the following model describing population-toxicant interactions in an advective environment:

{ut=d1​ux​x−a1​ux+u⁡(r−c​u−m​w),x∈(0,L),t>0,wt=d2​wx​x−a2​wx+h⁡(x)−q​w−p​u​w,x∈(0,L),t>0,d1​ux​(0,t)−a1​u​(0,t)=ux​(L,t)=0,t>0,d2​wx​(0,t)−a2​w​(0,t)=wx​(L,t)=0,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x)≥,≢0,w(x,0)=w0(x)≥,≢0.\begin{cases}u_{t}=d_{1}u_{xx}-a_{1}u_{x}+u\left(r-cu-mw\right),&x\in\left(0,L\right),t>0,\\ w_{t}=d_{2}w_{xx}-a_{2}w_{x}+h(x)-qw-puw,&x\in\left(0,L\right),t>0,\\ d_{1}u_{x}\left(0,t\right)-a_{1}u\left(0,t\right)=u_{x}\left(L,t\right)=0,&t>0,\\ d_{2}w_{x}\left(0,t\right)-a_{2}w\left(0,t\right)=w_{x}\left(L,t\right)=0,&t>0,\\ u\left(x,0\right)=u_{0}\left(x\right)\geq,\not\equiv 0,\\ w\left(x,0\right)=w_{0}\left(x\right)\geq,\not\equiv 0.\end{cases} (1.1)

Here u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) and w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) represent the population density and the toxicant concentration at location xx and time tt, respectively, and the function h⁡(x)h(x) is the rate of the exogenous input of the toxicant into the river. In (1.1), u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) and w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) satisfy a Robin condition at the upstream boundary x=0x=0 and a Neumann condition at the downstream boundary x=Lx=L. For the interpretations of d1,d2,r,c,m,p,q,L>0d_{1},d_{2},r,c,m,p,q,L>0 and a1,a2≥0a_{1},a_{2}\geq 0, one can refer to [32]. Based on eigenvalue analysis, [32] derived sufficient conditions for population persistence or extinction and numerically investigated the effects of factors like toxicant input, flow velocity, and diffusion/advection characteristics on population persistence and spatial distribution. With a change of variables and assume that h⁡(x)≡h>0h(x)\equiv h>0, model (1.1) can be rewritten as:

{ut=d1​ux​x−a1​ux+u⁡(r−u−m​w),x∈(0,L),t>0,wt=d2​wx​x−a2​wx+h−q​w−p​u​w,x∈(0,L),t>0,d1​ux​(0,t)−a1​u​(0,t)=ux​(L,t)=0,t>0,d2​wx​(0,t)−a2​w​(0,t)=wx​(L,t)=0,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x)≥,≢0,w(x,0)=w0(x)≥,≢0.\begin{cases}u_{t}=d_{1}u_{xx}-a_{1}u_{x}+u\left(r-u-mw\right),&x\in\left(0,L\right),t>0,\\ w_{t}=d_{2}w_{xx}-a_{2}w_{x}+h-qw-puw,&x\in\left(0,L\right),t>0,\\ d_{1}u_{x}\left(0,t\right)-a_{1}u\left(0,t\right)=u_{x}\left(L,t\right)=0,&t>0,\\ d_{2}w_{x}\left(0,t\right)-a_{2}w\left(0,t\right)=w_{x}\left(L,t\right)=0,&t>0,\\ u\left(x,0\right)=u_{0}\left(x\right)\geq,\not\equiv 0,\\ w\left(x,0\right)=w_{0}\left(x\right)\geq,\not\equiv 0.\end{cases} (1.2)

Wang [27] extensively analyzed the dependence of the toxicant-only semi-trivial steady state of model (1.2) on multiple parameters by classifying cases based on the presence of advection in the species, toxicant, or both. Xing et al. [29] extended model (1.1) by incorporating the assumption that populations tend to move away from high toxicant concentrations, introducing a toxicant-taxis term. Their study investigated the existence of positive steady states and the influence of chemotaxis and population advection velocity on the stability of the pure-toxicant steady state, offering novel insights into toxicant-population dynamics.

To enhance the survival prospects of aquatic organisms in polluted rivers or streams, establishing protected zones represents a key strategy. This involves engineered pollutant remediation and targeted detoxification within a designated river section. The objectives are twofold: to ensure that species inhabiting this zone can grow unimpeded by toxicant, and to maintain unrestricted diffusion of aquatic organisms within the protected area. Critical questions then arise: How does the implementation of such protected zones influence population persistence or extinction dynamics within contaminated riverine ecosystems? Furthermore, how do ecological factors modulate population responses under protected area regimes? To address these questions, inspired by related works on protection zones in predator-prey and competition models [1, 2, 3, 9, 15, 16, 25, 28, 30], we extend the framework of model (1.2) to investigate a population-toxicant model incorporating a protected zone. Empirical evidence suggests that establishing a single large protected area is generally more economical and practical than creating multiple smaller zones of equivalent total size [3]. Consequently, this study focuses on a population-toxicant model featuring a single protected zone. Specifically, we examine the ecological implications of situating this protected zone at two distinct locations: upstream and downstream.

A spatiotemporal model to assess the impact of toxicants on aquatic populations in a polluted river with a upstream protected zone under advective conditions is

{ut=d1​ux​x−a1​ux+u⁡(r−u−m​χ(x1,L]​w),x∈(0,L),t>0,wt=d2​wx​x−a2​wx+h−q​w−p​u​w,x∈(x1,L),t>0,d1​ux​(0,t)−a1​u​(0,t)=ux​(L,t)=0,t>0,d2​wx​(x1,t)−a2​w​(x1,t)=wx​(L,t)=0,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x)≥,≢0,0<x<L,w(x,0)=w0(x)≥,≢0,x1<x<L.\begin{cases}u_{t}=d_{1}u_{xx}-a_{1}u_{x}+u\left(r-u-m\chi_{\left(x_{1},L\right]}w\right),&x\in\left(0,L\right),t>0,\\ w_{t}=d_{2}w_{xx}-a_{2}w_{x}+h-qw-puw,&x\in\left(x_{1},L\right),t>0,\\ d_{1}u_{x}\left(0,t\right)-a_{1}u\left(0,t\right)=u_{x}\left(L,t\right)=0,&t>0,\\ d_{2}w_{x}\left(x_{1},t\right)-a_{2}w\left(x_{1},t\right)=w_{x}\left(L,t\right)=0,&t>0,\\ u\left(x,0\right)=u_{0}\left(x\right)\geq,\not\equiv 0,&0<x<L,\\ w\left(x,0\right)=w_{0}\left(x\right)\geq,\not\equiv 0,&x_{1}<x<L.\par\end{cases} (1.3)

Here, χ(x1,L]\chi_{\left(x_{1},L\right]} is defined as

χ(x1,L]={0,0≤x≤x1,1,x1<x≤L.\chi_{\left(x_{1},L\right]}=\begin{cases}0,&0\leq x\leq x_{1},\\ 1,&x_{1}<x\leq L.\end{cases}

This means that (0,x1)(0,x_{1}), imposed a Robin condition on the toxicant at x1x_{1}, represents a upstream protected zone where aquatic species are unaffected by toxicant.

Alternatively, a spatiotemporal model of populations exposed to toxicants in a polluted river featuring a downstream protected zone within an advective environment is

{ut=d1​ux​x−a1​ux+u⁡(r−u−m​χ[0,x2)​w),x∈(0,L),t>0,wt=d2​wx​x−a2​wx+h−q​w−p​u​w,x∈(0,x2),t>0,d1​ux​(0,t)−a1​u​(0,t)=ux​(L,t)=0,t>0,d2​wx​(0,t)−a2​w​(0,t)=d2​wx​(x2,t)−a2​w​(x2,t)=0,t>0,u(x,0)=u0(x)≥,≢0,0<x<L,w(x,0)=w0(x)≥,≢0,0<x<x2.\begin{cases}u_{t}=d_{1}u_{xx}-a_{1}u_{x}+u\left(r-u-m\chi_{\left[0,x_{2}\right)}w\right),&x\in\left(0,L\right),t>0,\\ w_{t}=d_{2}w_{xx}-a_{2}w_{x}+h-qw-puw,&x\in\left(0,x_{2}\right),t>0,\\ d_{1}u_{x}\left(0,t\right)-a_{1}u\left(0,t\right)=u_{x}\left(L,t\right)=0,&t>0,\\ d_{2}w_{x}\left(0,t\right)-a_{2}w\left(0,t\right)=d_{2}w_{x}\left(x_{2},t\right)-a_{2}w\left(x_{2},t\right)=0,&t>0,\\ u\left(x,0\right)=u_{0}\left(x\right)\geq,\not\equiv 0,&0<x<L,\\ w\left(x,0\right)=w_{0}\left(x\right)\geq,\not\equiv 0,&0<x<x_{2}.\end{cases} (1.4)

Here, χ[0,x2)\chi_{\left[0,x_{2}\right)} is defined as

χ[0,x2)={1,0≤x<x2,0,x2≤x≤L.\chi_{\left[0,x_{2}\right)}=\begin{cases}1,&0\leq x<x_{2},\\ 0,&x_{2}\leq x\leq L.\end{cases}

Then (x2,L)(x_{2},L), imposed a Robin condition on the toxicant at x2x_{2}, represents a downstream protected zone where aquatic species are unaffected by toxicant.

This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the main results for models (1.3) and (1.4). The proofs of these results are provided in Section 3. Section 4 numerically analyzes the combined effects of toxicant advection and protected zone size interactions on population persistence, as well as the distributions of the population and toxicant. Finally, Section 5 summarizes our conclusions and discusses future work.

2 Main results

Systems (1.3) and (1.4) admit a unique semi-trivial steady state, denoted by (0,w~)(0,\tilde{w}) and (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w}), respectively, where w~\tilde{w} and w¯\bar{w} will be defined in Lemma 3.1. Similarly to [27, 32], the following proposition on the global dynamics of systems (1.3) and (1.4) is true.

Proposition A.
(i)(i)

If system (1.3) (resp. (1.4)) has no positive steady states, then the semi-trivial steady state (0,w~)(0,\tilde{w}) (resp. (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w})) is globally asymptotically stable among all nonnegative and nontrivial initial conditions.

(i​i)(ii)

If the semi-trivial steady state (0,w~)(0,\tilde{w}) (resp. (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w})) is linearly unstable, then system (1.3) (resp.(1.4)) has at least one local stable coexistence steady state; Furthermore, if every coexistence steady state is linearly stable, then there is a unique coexistence steady state which is globally asymptotically stable among all nonnegative and nontrivial initial conditions.

Theorem 2.1 shows that the population face extinction due to its large advection rate (a1≥4​d1​ra_{1}\geq\sqrt{4d_{1}r}) or small advection rate while a short habitat length (0<a1<4​d1​r0<a_{1}<\sqrt{4d_{1}r}, L<L1∗L<L^{*}_{1}). When the advection rate of the population is small (0<a1<4​d1​r0<a_{1}<\sqrt{4d_{1}r}) and the river length is large (L>L1∗)(L>L_{1}^{*}), Theorem 2.1 characterizes the influence of upstream protection zone length on the stability of the equilibrium (0,w~)(0,\tilde{w}) (see Figure 1). Specifically,

  • •

    When the protected area exceeds a critical spatial threshold (x1≥L∗)(x_{1}\geq L^{*}), population persistence occurs irrespective of toxicant exposure levels.

  • •

    Below this threshold (x1<L∗)(x_{1}<L^{*}), persistence becomes dependent on additional factors. Specifically, if any of the following occurs: the toxicant effect coefficient on population growth (mm) is sufficiently high, the contaminant discharge rate per unit (qq) is sufficiently low, or the toxicant input rate (hh) is sufficiently high, then a larger critical protection zone size is required to ensure persistence.

Moreover, d1∗​(r)d_{1}^{*}(r) is continuous and strictly increases for r∈(0,r∗)r\in(0,r^{*}) with limr→0d1∗​(r)=0\lim\limits_{r\to{0}}d_{1}^{*}(r)=0 and limr→r∗d1∗​(r)=+∞.\lim\limits_{r\to{r^{*}}}d_{1}^{*}(r)=+\infty.

Theorem 2.3 characterizes the effects of the advection rate a1a_{1}, the diffusion coefficient d1d_{1}, and the natural growth rate rr of population uu on its persistence (see Figure 3). That is

  • •

    High intrinsic growth rate (r≥r∗)(r\geq r^{*}): For fixed diffusion coefficient d1d_{1}, population persistence becomes advection-dependent. Survival occurs at low advection rates (0<a1<a1∗0<a_{1}<a_{1}^{*}), while extinction occurs at high advection rates (a1>a1∗a_{1}>a_{1}^{*}).

  • •

    Low intrinsic growth rate (r<r∗r<r^{*}): Extinction occurs for large diffusion coefficient (d1≥d1∗​(r)d_{1}\geq d_{1}^{*}(r)). If the diffusion coefficient is small (d1<d1∗​(r)d_{1}<d_{1}^{*}(r)), a small advection rate (0<a1<a1∗)(0<a_{1}<a_{1}^{*}) is beneficial for the population persistence.

About the existence of a positive steady state (u,w)(u,w) for system (1.3) and its stability, we have the following results.

Theorem 2.4.

Suppose that 0<a1<4​d1​r0<a_{1}<\sqrt{4d_{1}r} and L>L1∗L>L_{1}^{*}.

(i)(i)

For x1≥L∗x_{1}\geq L^{*} (large protection zone), when m≤p−1​e−|a1d1−a2d2|​Lm\leq p^{-1}e^{-|\frac{a_{1}}{d_{1}}-\frac{a_{2}}{d_{2}}|L} and w~2​(L)≤h\tilde{w}^{2}(L)\leq h, system (1.3) possesses a unique coexistence steady state (u,w)(u,w), which is globally asymptotically stable;

(i​i)(ii)

For x1<L∗x_{1}<L^{*} (small protection zone), when m<m​i​n​{m∗,p−1​e−|a1d1−a2d2|​L}m<min\{m^{*},p^{-1}e^{-|\frac{a_{1}}{d_{1}}-\frac{a_{2}}{d_{2}}|L}\} and w~2​(L)≤h\tilde{w}^{2}(L)\leq h, system (1.3) possesses a unique coexistence steady state (u,w)(u,w), which is globally asymptotically stable.

Next, we give some main results for system (1.4) which are analogous to Theorem 2.1, 2.3 and 2.4. About the influence of downstream protected zone length on the stability of the equilibrium of (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w}), we have the following results.

Theorem 2.5.

If a1≥4​d1​ra_{1}\geq\sqrt{4d_{1}r} or 0<a1<4​d1​r0<a_{1}<\sqrt{4d_{1}r} and L<L1∗L<L^{*}_{1}, then (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w}) is globally asymptotically stable; If 0<a1<4​d1​r0<a_{1}<\sqrt{4d_{1}r} and L>L1∗L>L_{1}^{*}, then the following results hold:

(i)(i)

If L−x2≥L∗L-x_{2}\geq L^{*} (large protection zone), then (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w}) is unstable;

(i​i)(ii)

If L−x2<L∗L-x_{2}<L^{*} (small protection zone), then the following statements are true:

(i​i​.1)(ii.1)

If all parameters except for hh and mm are fixed, and (h,m)∈{h>0,m>m¯​(h)}(h,m)\in\{h>0,m>\bar{m}(h)\}, then (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w}) is linearly stable; while for (h,m)∈{h>0,0<m<m¯(h)}(h,m)\in\{h>0,0<m<\bar{m}(h)\}, (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w}) is unstable.

(i​i​.2)(ii.2)

If all parameters except for qq and mm are fixed, and (q,m)∈{0<q<q¯(m),m>0}(q,m)\in\{0<q<\bar{q}(m)\text{,}m>0\}, then (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w}) is linearly stable; while for (q,m)∈{q>q¯​(m),m>0}(q,m)\in\{q>\bar{q}(m),m>0\}, (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w}) is unstable.

If the protected zone is situated at the downstream of the river, Theorem 2.5 shows that the population also face extinction due to its large advection rate (a1≥4​d1​ra_{1}\geq\sqrt{4d_{1}r}) or small advection rate while a short habitat length (0<a1<4​d1​r0<a_{1}<\sqrt{4d_{1}r}, L<L1∗L<L^{*}_{1}). When the advection rate of the population is small (0<a1<4​d1​r0<a_{1}<\sqrt{4d_{1}r}) and the river length is large (L>L1∗)(L>L_{1}^{*}), Theorem 2.5 characterizes the influence of downstream protected zone length on the stability of the equilibrium (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w}). Specifically, when the protected area exceeds a critical spatial threshold (L−x2≥L∗)(L-x_{2}\geq L^{*}), population persistence occurs irrespective of toxicant exposure levels; Below this threshold (L−x2<L∗)(L-x_{2}<L^{*}), persistence becomes dependent on additional factors: the effect coefficient of toxicant on population growth mm, per-unit contaminant discharge rate qq, and toxicant input rate hh.

For system (1.4), the following results show the effects of the advection rate a1a_{1}, the diffusion coefficient d1d_{1}, and the natural growth rate rr of population uu on its persistence.

Theorem 2.6.

Assume that all parameters except for a1a_{1}, d1d_{1} and rr are fixed. Let r¯=m​∫0x2w¯​𝑑xL\bar{r}=\frac{m\int_{0}^{x_{2}}\bar{w}dx}{L}. Then we have the following results:

(i)(i)

If r≥r¯r\geq\bar{r}, given d1d_{1}, then there exists a¯1>0\bar{a}_{1}>0 satisfying λ1​(d1,a¯1,r−m​χ[0,x2)​w¯,(0,L))=0\lambda_{1}(d_{1},\bar{a}_{1},r-m\chi_{\left[0,x_{2}\right)}\bar{w},\left(0,L\right))=0 such that (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w}) is linearly stable when a1>a¯1a_{1}>\bar{a}_{1}, and unstable when 0<a1<a¯10<a_{1}<\bar{a}_{1};

(i​i)(ii)

If r<r¯r<\bar{r}, then there exists d¯1>0\bar{d}_{1}>0 satisfying λ1​(d¯1,0,r−m​χ[0,x2)​w¯,(0,L))=0\lambda_{1}\left(\bar{d}_{1},0,r-m\chi_{\left[0,x_{2}\right)}\bar{w},\left(0,L\right)\right)=0 such that the following statements are true:

(i​i​.1)(ii.1)

If d1≥d¯1​(r)d_{1}\geq\bar{d}_{1}(r), then (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w}) is linearly stable for any a1>0a_{1}>0;

(i​i​.2)(ii.2)

If d1<d¯1​(r)d_{1}<\bar{d}_{1}(r), then (0,w¯)(0,\bar{w}) is linearly stable for a1>a¯1a_{1}>\bar{a}_{1}, and unstable for 0<a1<a¯10<a_{1}<\bar{a}_{1}.

Moreover, d¯1​(r)\bar{d}_{1}(r) is a continuous function of rr and strictly decrease for r∈(0,r¯)r\in(0,\bar{r}) with limr→0d¯1​(r)=0,limr→r¯d¯1​(r)=+∞.\lim\limits_{r\to{0}}\bar{d}_{1}(r)=0,\quad\lim\limits_{r\to{\bar{r}}}\bar{d}_{1}(r)=+\infty.

Theorem 2.6 implies that if the intrinsic growth rate rr is sufficiently large, then a low advection rate a1a_{1} promotes population persistence; If the intrinsic growth rate rr is small, then both a low diffusion rate d1d_{1} and a low advection rate a1a_{1} are required to ensure population persistence.

The following results show that, under some sufficient conditions, system (1.4) admits a unique coexistence steady state, which is globally asymptotically stable.

Theorem 2.7.

Suppose that 0<a1<4​d1​r0<a_{1}<\sqrt{4d_{1}r} and L>L1∗L>L_{1}^{*}. Then the following statements hold:

(i)(i)

For L−x2≥L∗L-x_{2}\geq L^{*} (large protection zone), when m≤p−1​e−|a1d1−a2d2|​x2m\leq p^{-1}e^{-|\frac{a_{1}}{d_{1}}-\frac{a_{2}}{d_{2}}|x_{2}} and w¯2​(x2)≤h\bar{w}^{2}(x_{2})\leq h, system (1.4) possesses a unique coexistence steady state (u,w)(u,w) which is globally asymptotically stable;

(i​i)(ii)

For L−x2<L∗L-x_{2}<L^{*} (small protection zone), when m<m​i​n​{m¯,p−1​e−|a1d1−a2d2|​x2}m<min\{\bar{m},p^{-1}e^{-|\frac{a_{1}}{d_{1}}-\frac{a_{2}}{d_{2}}|x_{2}}\} and w¯2​(x2)≤h\bar{w}^{2}(x_{2})\leq h, system (1.4) possesses a unique coexistence steady state (u,w)(u,w) which is globally asymptotically stable.

5 Conclusion

To protect aquatic species in polluted rivers, this paper develops a reaction-diffusion-advection model for population-toxicant interactions. The model incorporates Danckwerts boundary conditions and two types of boundary protection zones. For both upstream and downstream protection zone configurations, analysis of toxicant-only steady states yields conditions for population persistence. Furthermore, applying monotone dynamical system theory and eigenvalue analysis, we derive a sufficient condition for the global asymptotic stability of the coexistence steady state.

Specifically, this paper focuses on the comprehensive effects of the size of the protection zone (x1x_{1}/L−x2L-x_{2}), the population diffusion rate (d1d_{1}), the population/toxicant advection rate (a1a_{1}/a2a_{2}), the intrinsic growth rate of the population (rr), the toxicant input rate (hh), the toxicant effect coefficient on population growth (mm), and the contaminant discharge rate per unit (qq) on the persistence of the population.

Our study shows that the population face extinction due to its large advection rate (a1≥4​d1​ra_{1}\geq\sqrt{4d_{1}r}) or a small advection rate while a short habitat length (0<a1<4​d1​r0<a_{1}<\sqrt{4d_{1}r}, L<L1∗L<L^{*}_{1}) no matter the protected zone is situated at the upstream or the downstream of the river. When the advection rate of the population is small and the river length is large (0<a1​<4​d1​r,L>​L1∗)(0<a_{1}<\sqrt{4d_{1}r},L>L_{1}^{*}), the persistence of the population is determined by the combined interaction of the protection zone length and other biological parameters. Specifically,

  • •

    When the protected area exceeds a critical spatial threshold (x1≥L∗x_{1}\geq L^{*}, resp. L−x2≥L∗L-x_{2}\geq L^{*}), population persistence occurs irrespective of toxicant exposure levels.

  • •

    Below this threshold (x1<L∗x_{1}<L^{*}, resp. L−x2<L∗L-x_{2}<L^{*}), persistence becomes dependent on additional factors. Specifically, if any of the following occurs: the toxicant effect coefficient on population growth (mm) is sufficiently high, the contaminant discharge rate per unit (qq) is sufficiently low, or the toxicant input rate (hh) is sufficiently high, then a larger critical protection zone size is required to ensure persistence.

For a fixed protection zone,

  • •

    When the toxicant input hh or the effect of toxicant on population growth mm is low, or the contaminant export rate qq is high, population uu persists regardless of toxicant advection. Conversely, high hh or mm, or low qq, induces habitat-dependent survival: the population persists at high a2a_{2} but goes extinct at low a2a_{2}.

  • •

    For sufficiently small m,h>0m,h>0, the population uu can always persist. The critical contamination threshold for the persistence of population uu decreases monotonically with increasing mm.

  • •

    For fixed m>0m>0, the population uu can always persist when qq is sufficiently large. The critical detoxification threshold increases monotonically with mm.

  • •

    If the intrinsic growth rate rr is sufficiently large, then a low advection rate a1a_{1} promotes population persistence; If the intrinsic growth rate rr is small, then both a low diffusion rate d1d_{1} and a low advection rate a1a_{1} are required to ensure population persistence.

Some of our future work will focus on extending the mathematical modeling and analysis to address the following issues: (1) The impact of the protection zone on population dynamics under spatially heterogeneous exogenous toxicant input rates into the river; (2) The influence of the protection zone on population dynamics when considering alternative boundary conditions. A deeper investigation into these questions will provide enhanced scientific and theoretical support for water resource and environmental management authorities. This will facilitate improved monitoring and management of species diversity within aquatic ecosystems, ultimately contributing to the optimization of ecological conservation strategies.
